content:
Unsigned owner receives call from bank claiming option chosen, next day told bank got it wrong

The first deadline for Wang Fuk Court owners to submit acceptance letters for the government's acquisition proposal ended on 30 June. Wang Chi House, where over 75% of owners indicated willingness to sell their titles, has been included in the long-term residency scheme. The government said that as of the 16th of this month, it had signed sale and purchase agreements with 769 households.

Mr Chan, who lives on a mid-floor unit of Wang Chi House, bought his flat in 2017 and has about HK$2 million remaining on his mortgage. He has not yet signed and returned the "acceptance of acquisition proposal letter". He told Re-news Agency last Monday (the 13th) that day he received a call from a staff member of Standard Chartered Bank, which handles his mortgage. The caller said they had been informed by the government that he had chosen "Plan B"—the option of taking the money and purchasing a new Home Ownership Scheme flat.

Mr Chan immediately made clear he had never signed or returned the acquisition letter, questioned whether the caller had got it wrong, and asked for the information to be checked. The staff member repeated his address, reaffirmed it was a government notification, explained the mortgage arrangements after the title was sold, and said they would record Mr Chan's situation and inform their supervisor.

The next day (the 14th), Mr Chan received another call from the same staff member, who said that after checking with the bank and verifying the information provided by the government, they found the bank had "got it wrong"—according to the government's data he had not chosen "Plan B"—and apologised to him.

Worried about being "misrepresented" and lacking information, he has not responded

Mr Chan told Re-news Agency that he has not signed the acquisition letter because the authorities have yet to answer questions on repair cost arrangements, insurance compensation, and whether repairs will be carried out to allow residents to return to Wang Chi House. With too many uncertainties, he cannot decide to sell his title at this stage: "It's not like you say sell and I just sell." He believes the long-term residency scheme, which relies on a ballot and uses integrated modular construction of inconsistent quality, is not attractive enough for him to prioritise selling.

After it was earlier announced that over 75% of Wang Chi House owners were willing to accept the acquisition, Mr Chan became suspicious. He pointed out that many people in the neighbourhood group chat said they would not sell, and felt the figures were "just what they say" while "no one knows what goes on in the middle". He said frankly: "If they voted at an owners' meeting and announced the result on the spot, then I'd believe it." Out of fear of being "misrepresented" or taken out of context, he has refrained from any response.

"No matter what I decide, I'll still have to sell to them"

Mr Chan was astonished by the bank's first call: "I never chose anything, yet the government went and told the bank I'd picked Plan B." He gave a wry smile: "So I'm one of that 75%. I keep telling people I'm not, wondering who's in that 75%—turns out I am, and I didn't even know I'd become one of them."

Mr Chan stressed that the fairest approach would be to vote on the spot at an owners' meeting and announce the result immediately, but the Hop On Alliance has said the meeting will not handle the matter of selling titles. He suspects the authorities are "afraid that if there's an immediate vote, they won't be able to wriggle out of it". He sighed that this incident has reinforced his feeling that "no matter how I decide, in the end the government will use its methods to make me sell to them—it's just a matter of whether I sell sooner or later."

Even the bank's next-day call saying it had "got it wrong" has not fully allayed Mr Chan's doubts. He said: "They say what they say, I listen."

Even more unwilling to sell after the owners' meeting

Mr Chan understands the scheme will not change, but still hopes to find out whether there is a repair option that would allow residents to return to Wang Chi House, whose units have not yet been destroyed. "Until it's officially announced, we still have a chance that it really can be repaired." He also said that if the government ultimately enacts legislation to acquire the property, he will have to sell anyway, but if the government does not acquire his title, "you have to let me go back up and live there."

At the owners' meeting held on Sunday (the 19th), Mr Chan questioned whether its nature was lawful, saying it was merely "doing homework" and avoiding residents' questions—"it only talks about what it wants to talk about". He said he is even less willing to sell his title to the government after the owners' meeting, because insurance compensation could have been used to repair Wang Chi House, but once the title is sold, the insurance compensation will go to the government.

Housing Bureau: Cases with outstanding mortgages to be referred to banks after letters received

Re-news Agency made enquiries to the Housing Bureau last Monday (the 13th) on whether it was aware of the incident, whether it involved an error by the bureau, whether similar cases existed, whether it would affect previously announced figures, and how residents could be reassured. The bureau did not give a direct response, and only replied yesterday (the 20th) that, according to the Hong Kong Monetary Authority and the Hong Kong Banking Association's announcement in March this year, the HKMA, the Banking Association and the banking industry would set up a communication platform—including through the Housing Bureau-coordinated "explanation team"—to understand the specific needs of Wang Fuk Court residents and provide suitable assistance for each case.

The bureau said it has been maintaining close communication with the Banking Association and banks involved in mortgages on Wang Fuk Court units. Upon receiving the duly signed "acceptance of acquisition proposal letter" from an owner, the explanation team will, based on the mortgage information provided in the letter, and for cases where the mortgage has not yet been fully repaid, refer those cases to the mortgagee bank in accordance with the personal data collection statement contained in the letter, so the bank can assign dedicated staff to contact the owner, help them understand the special mortgage arrangements the industry offers to assist owners, and provide appropriate assistance.

Standard Chartered: No comment on individual cases, handled with empathy

A Standard Chartered Bank spokesperson replied on Tuesday last week (the 14th) that it would not comment on individual customer cases, adding that it has a dedicated team that follows up with empathy according to the individual needs of affected Wang Fuk Court owner-customers, and ensures that customer data is handled properly.

The first batch deadline for Wang Fuk Court acquisitions ended on 30 June. Deputy Financial Secretary Michael Wong said recently that as of the 16th of this month, 1,786 households had signed and returned the "acceptance of acquisition proposal letter", accounting for over 90% of all households, of which approximately 43%—that is, 769 households—had signed sale and purchase agreements.
